moduleTitle: Optimizing Test Execution in Tricentis Testim
learningObjectives: List the benefits of running multiple tests locally, using the Scheduler, and running tests in Incognito mode with Testim IO.
Use a configuration file with the Testim CLI, and interpret test results, test duration, run configuration, and test parameters.
Describe the Execution Run view and Test Runs view to analyze statistics of past tests run by local suite, CI, or Scheduler.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Running multiple tests locally and on a schedule

elements.description: From Test List > Tests, selecting several tests and running them takes control of your mouse and runs the selected tests sequentially in your local Chrome browser (local runs are Chrome-only). Because Testim is actively driving the browser, you should not use your mouse or computer while the tests run. Locally-run tests are tracked and viewable afterward under Runs > Executions, tagged 'local-suite'.

elements.text: Treat browser/session cleanup as a diagnostic check if a local batch stalls. An unclosed browser alone does not establish that the next test must fail; inspect the actual error and lifecycle evidence.

elements.description: Scheduler runs selected labels, suites or test plans on a schedule, with applicable grid, branch and configuration. It can coexist with CI. Test plans supply their own grid/base URL/configuration, so those overrides are not available in the scheduler. Clone a schedule and review the copied settings.

bulletPoints: Local Test List web playback uses Chrome and takes control of input.
Investigate actual browser/session evidence when a batch fails.
Scheduler supports labels, suites or test plans; plan-owned settings restrict overrides.
Built-in scheduling is useful with or without an existing CI pipeline.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Incognito mode and the Configuration File

elements.description: Incognito isolates browser cookies, login state and autocomplete from ordinary sessions. Enable the Testim extension in Incognito before local use. It does not reset backend data or guarantee an entirely fresh application/account state.

A CLI configuration file supplies execution options, parameters and hooks; it is not automatic encryption. Use supported Secrets Manager references instead of literal credentials. Static JSON params files need the documented JavaScript/module.exports conversion for secret references. Screenshot masking applies only to password-type fields, so review artifacts separately.

bulletPoints: Incognito isolates browser state; backend/account reset is separate.
Configuration supports options/hooks and secret references, without automatically encrypting literal values.

elements.description: CLI --timeout uses milliseconds; Scheduler Test timeout uses seconds. Both document a 10-minute default and three-hour maximum. Do not confuse this test limit with the execution-list status that can temporarily become Timeout after 90 minutes while grid work continues.

CLI documentation describes timeout-specific retries up to three times and --disable-timeout-retry. Scheduler documentation describes one extra timeout run and its disable toggle. Check the actual execution path/version rather than promising one universal retry count.

General failed-test retries use their configured maximum and stop on success. They are separate from timeout retries; passing after retry is evidence to investigate, not proof the original defect or instability is fixed.

bulletPoints: Test timeout units differ: CLI milliseconds, Scheduler seconds.
CLI and Scheduler timeout-retry descriptions differ; inspect the chosen path.
A 90-minute execution-list Timeout can be temporary, not proof grid work stopped.
General retries are bounded and do not fix the underlying cause.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Diagnosing a failure and reading the Execution Runs view

elements.description: For visual symptoms, compare available baseline and result screenshots alongside the failed step, error and environment. Screenshots do not establish every network, credential or backend cause; gather relevant evidence before changing configuration.

The execution list shows duration, parallel test concurrency and results. Its graph plots execution count over time, not duration. Execution details include source/version/grid/data evidence; the details’ concurrent-executions count is distinct from the list’s parallel-test count.

bulletPoints: Use screenshots with error and environment evidence for diagnosis.
Distinguish execution-count graph, list concurrency and detailed execution metadata.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: The Test Runs view: statistics across past runs

elements.description: The Test Runs screen shows statistics on past runs — aggregated across all selected tests, and per-test (e.g. how many times a specific test passed/failed and its average test duration) — under the Test statistics section. Filters (status, time, execution/label) narrow what's shown, and clicking a specific run opens it in the Test Editor to drill into per-step screenshots and durations.

elements.term: Counted runs vs. Local Editor Runs
elements.description: Test Runs separates Counted Runs from Local Editor Runs. Under the documented test-runs subscription model, local editor runs are exempt; local library/CLI executions and remote grid runs are counted. A remote grid run launched from the editor must not be treated as quota-free solely because the editor triggered it.

bulletPoints: Filtered Test Runs statistics show pass counts and average duration.
Counted runs include applicable local and remote executions.
The quota exemption is for local editor runs, not every editor-triggered remote run.

examPitfalls.title: Confusing timeout retry with failed-test retry
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming the automatic timeout retry (up to 3x, timeout-specific) is the same mechanism as general failed-test retries.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Separate timeout-specific retries from configured general retries. CLI describes up to three timeout retries; Scheduler describes one extra run. Verify the chosen path and disable controls.

examPitfalls.title: Setting timeout so low it fails legitimately slow flows
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Leaving or setting an aggressive timeout on a test that includes a genuinely slow operation (large file processing, a heavy report generation), causing false failures.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The timeout can be extended up to 3 hours for scenarios that need it — extend it deliberately for known-slow flows rather than treating every timeout failure as a flaky test.

examPitfalls.title: Touching the mouse/keyboard during a local multi-test run
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Interacting with the machine while Testim is driving the local browser through a batch of tests from the Test List.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Testim takes control of the mouse during a local multi-test run — leave the mouse and keyboard alone until the run finishes, or risk interfering with the automation and causing spurious failures.

examPitfalls.title: Hardcoding a password into a step instead of using the Configuration File
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Typing a real credential directly into a step's value field, where it's stored in plain text and shows up in version history.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use supported secret references and protect configuration files; moving a literal password into a file does not encrypt it. Verify artifact exposure, including non-password fields.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming editor runs count toward the same Test Runs statistics as CI/Scheduler runs
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Expecting a quick ad-hoc run from the editor to show up in the main Test Runs (counted runs) numbers alongside CI/CLI/Scheduler executions.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Distinguish local editor playback from counted local library/CLI and remote grid runs under the documented subscription model.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A local Test List batch stalls after its first test. Browser cleanup is suspected but not yet verified. What is the supported diagnostic approach?

options.text: Assume the next test must succeed regardless of session state.
Inspect the browser/session lifecycle and the actual failure before concluding its cause.
Assume the CLI automatically fixes a Test List local run.
Assume a manual trigger is always required between tests.

practiceQuiz.hint: A suspected lifecycle problem is not a proven root cause.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Inspect the actual local run and session evidence. The source documents local Chrome batch playback and input control, not a guaranteed next-test failure from an unclosed browser alone.

optionExplanations.A: No session-state-independent success guarantee is established.
optionExplanations.B: Inspecting actual evidence tests the suspected lifecycle cause.
optionExplanations.C: Local Test List playback is not automatically repaired by a CLI runner.
optionExplanations.D: The documented batch workflow does not require a manual trigger between every test.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Your team wants nightly scheduled tests without requiring a CI pipeline to trigger them. Which scenario matches Scheduler’s purpose?

options.text: When your team utilizes CI tools such as Jenkins, Bamboo, or similar
When your team needs to execute tests immediately without any scheduling
When your team lacks CI tools and needs to manually schedule test executions
When you need to run tests without any labels

practiceQuiz.hint: It's built-in scheduling that doesn't require a CI/CD pipeline.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Scheduler provides built-in scheduled execution and can coexist with CI. Select supported labels, suites or plans and the applicable configuration; lacking CI is not a prerequisite for using it.

optionExplanations.A: CI presence alone does not explain the requested nightly scheduling need.
optionExplanations.B: Immediate ad-hoc execution is not the stated requirement.
optionExplanations.C: Built-in scheduling satisfies the stated need without requiring a CI trigger.
optionExplanations.D: Scheduler selects supported labels, suites or plans, not arbitrary unlabeled tests.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the primary benefit of running tests in Incognito mode in Testim?

options.text: Browser session isolation from ordinary saved cookies and login state.
Tests can save log-in states
Tests can access stored cookies
Tests run faster on execution

practiceQuiz.hint: It's about a clean starting point, not speed or persistence.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Incognito isolates ordinary browser session state. It does not reset backend records or guarantee account/application state; extension permission and suitable configuration are still needed.

optionExplanations.A: Incognito isolates ordinary saved browser session state.
optionExplanations.B: Persisting ordinary login state is not the isolation benefit.
optionExplanations.C: Reusing ordinary saved cookies is not the stated benefit.
optionExplanations.D: Incognito does not guarantee faster execution.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which describes using a Testim CLI configuration file with supported secret references?

options.text: It can supply run options/hooks and secret references, without automatically encrypting literal credentials.
It locates the test data is available on the local system
It provides test scripts for any web application
It allows users to log out automatically after the test run is finished.

practiceQuiz.hint: Execution configuration and secret management are distinct mechanisms.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Configuration files supply options and hooks and can reference managed secrets. They do not automatically encrypt literals; secret-reference params files and screenshot masking have documented limits.

optionExplanations.A: It supplies execution options/hooks and managed-secret references with documented limits.
optionExplanations.B: Its role is not automatic discovery of all local data.
optionExplanations.C: It does not generate scripts for arbitrary applications.
optionExplanations.D: Logout requires the appropriate application workflow or hook logic.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A failed step appears to target the wrong visible control, and baseline/result screenshots are available. Which listed action provides useful visual evidence before changing the environment?

options.text: Immediately re-run the test without changing anything
Ignore the error message and check only the console logs
Compare the baseline screenshot with the result screenshot
Change the test resolution and run it on a different browser

practiceQuiz.hint: Visual comparison is one of the most direct ways to see what actually happened.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Compare available screenshots with the failed-step error and target evidence. This helps investigate the stated visual symptom; it is not a universal root-cause diagnosis for every failure.

optionExplanations.A: A blind replay does not inspect the available failure evidence.
optionExplanations.B: Ignoring the error discards useful evidence.
optionExplanations.C: Available screenshots help investigate the stated visible target mismatch.
optionExplanations.D: Changing environment before inspecting evidence obscures the original symptom.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which combination is explicitly present in the Execution Runs list’s Duration, Concurrency and Results fields?

options.text: Duration, concurrency, number of passed and failed tests
Browser used, duration, concurrency, and URL
Suite label, duration, total tests, and start time
Scheduler, CLI version, logs, and test results

practiceQuiz.hint: These are list fields; the graph instead shows execution count over time.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The list includes duration, concurrent test count and passed/failed results. The execution graph plots execution count over time, while detailed hover metadata supplies additional source/version/grid/data evidence.

optionExplanations.A: These are the listed duration, parallel-test concurrency and results fields.
optionExplanations.B: URL is additional detail, not this requested combination of list fields.
optionExplanations.C: This lacks the requested concurrency and results combination.
optionExplanations.D: This is not the named trio of list fields.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Where would you check the average duration of test runs in Testim?

options.text: Test statistics
Run Graph
Filters Panel
Test retries section

practiceQuiz.hint: It's the same section that shows pass/fail counts per test.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The Test Runs screen's Test statistics section displays aggregated and per-test statistics — including the number of times a test passed/failed and its average test duration. The Filters panel narrows what's shown but doesn't itself display duration, and there's no dedicated 'test retries section' for this.

optionExplanations.A: The statistics section includes average duration.
optionExplanations.B: The graph shows individual run durations, not this aggregated statistic.
optionExplanations.C: Filters choose the data scope rather than supply the average themselves.
optionExplanations.D: Retry inspection is separate from the aggregated duration statistic.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Under the documented test-runs subscription model, which run type is exempt from the quota and tracked as Local Editor Runs?

options.text: Tests run by CLI
Tests run by CI tools
Tests run by Scheduled Runs
A test played locally from the editor.

practiceQuiz.hint: It's tracked in its own separate tab instead.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Local editor playback is exempt. Applicable local library/CLI and remote grid runs count; the editor as a trigger does not make a remote run quota-free.

optionExplanations.A: CLI executions are included in the documented quota model.
optionExplanations.B: CI-triggered runs are included in that model.
optionExplanations.D: Local editor playback is the documented exemption.

quickRecap.value: Local library web playback uses Chrome and input control; inspect session lifecycle evidence if it fails.
Built-in scheduled labels/suites/plans can coexist with CI; test plans own some execution settings.
Isolate browser session state; do not assume backend/account reset.
Run options/hooks and secret references; literal values are not automatically encrypted.
CLI timeout uses ms; Scheduler uses seconds. Retry descriptions differ by path; general retries are separate.
Use available screenshots with error and environment evidence.
Graph: execution count over time. List: duration, parallel tests and results.
Local editor playback is exempt under the documented model; applicable local/remote executions count.
